messages.content: Write a post about what a software company learned from a year of remote work. Around 250 words.

A year of remote work taught us that most of what we assumed going in was wrong.

We started by moving the office onto video calls: daily standups, back-to-back meetings, a chat channel for every team. People kept showing up. They said less each time. It took months to see the real problem — we'd kept the meetings but lost the hallway talk that used to make them short.

The fix wasn't another tool. We cut recurring meetings in half and had every team post a short daily update instead: what shipped, what's stuck, what's next. Engineers read them on their own schedule, not someone else's. Two quarters later, cycle time on tickets fell 18%, and nobody asked for the old meetings back.

Time zones stopped being something to route around. We gave each project a home time zone and let async updates cover the rest, and cross-team handoffs stopped losing a full day waiting for a reply.

The lesson that stuck: showing up isn't the same as working, and a full calendar isn't the same as collaborating. What actually moved the numbers was writing things down, trusting people to read them, and giving back the hours that used to disappear into meetings nobody wanted.

We're still figuring pieces of this out. But a year in, the team ships faster with fewer meetings than it ever did in the office.
